description_full: Starwood Property Trust, Inc. operates as a real estate investment trust (REIT) in the United States and internationally. It operates through four segments: Commercial and Residential Lending; Infrastructure Lending; Property; and Investing and Servicing. The Commercial and Residential Lending segment originates, acquires, finances, and manages commercial first mortgages, non-agency residential mortgages, subordinated mortgages, mezzanine loans, preferred equity, commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS), and residential mortgage-backed securities, as well as other real estate and real estate-related debt investments, including distressed or non-performing loans. Its Infrastructure Lending segment originates, acquires, finances, and manages infrastructure debt investments. The Property segment engages primarily in acquiring and managing equity interests in stabilized and to be stabilized commercial real estate properties, including multifamily properties, multi-tenant medical office net lease properties and diversified single-tenant triple net lease properties that are held for investment. Its Investing and Servicing segment manages and works out problem assets; acquires and manages unrated, investment grade, and non-investment grade rated CMBS comprising subordinated interests of securitization and re-securitization transactions; originates conduit loans for the primary purpose of selling these loans into securitization transactions; and acquires commercial real estate assets that include properties acquired from CMBS trusts. The company qualifies as a REIT for federal income tax purposes and would not be subject to federal corporate income taxes if it distributes at least 90% of its taxable income to its stockholders. Starwood Property Trust, Inc. was incorporated in 2009 and is headquartered in Miami Beach, Florida.

financial_summary: STARWOOD PROPERTY TRUST, INC. S is a mid-cap real estate business with a $4.2B market cap on $1.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $99M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.38× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 0.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield of 2.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 6.0% of the shares.

Remote work structural vacancy — the post-pandemic shift to hybrid work has permanently impaired demand for urban office space across most markets.
Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 26% operating margin is roughly in line with the Real Estate median (23%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.31x).
It accounts for 0.5% of sector revenue and 0.7% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-7.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 22% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 39% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 20% and a beta of 0.89, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.26 vs 5y 0.87), so read it loosely.
About $65.8M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.7x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 66% in the 2020 crash and 24% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 79% below its DCF fair value of $54.25, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 68%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $44.50 to $67.05 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Real Estate peers: cheaper on P/E 6.7 vs 23.9, richer on P/FCF 42.6 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 26% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 8 covering analysts target $17.31 on average, 53% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.51).
It converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow, or 2% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.38x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 5%.
ROE of 6% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (9.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.3% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.10 in the distress zone.
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 1.3 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.0% over 3 years, 10.2% over 5 years and 9.6% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 7.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -37.2% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of -1.3% a year over five years.
Capex runs 11.1x depreciation (47.6% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 6.0%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 56%.
It returns 2.4% a year to shareholders (16.9% in dividends, less 13.4% of net share issuance).
The share count has grown 3.6% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It pays out 320% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 324 employees, each generates about $5.7M of revenue, 2.5x the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 10.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $307K of free cash flow per employee.
